title: FAR U1·W3 — PP&E: Capitalization, Depreciation & Impairment (CPA Core · from CMA m4/m11)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — what goes into the cost of MBG's excavator?

Property, plant, and equipment is a heavily tested FAR area and a daily MBG decision: what is capitalized, how it is depreciated, and when it is written down. The CMA program treated the depreciation tax shield (month 11) as a cash flow; FAR governs the financial-accounting measurement underneath it.

Capitalization — what is included in cost

The cost of an asset includes its purchase price plus all costs necessary to get it ready for its intended use: freight-in, installation, testing, sales tax, and (for self-constructed assets) directly attributable labor, materials, and overhead. Avoidable interest on borrowings during the construction of a qualifying asset is capitalized (interest capitalization), not expensed. After acquisition, repairs and maintenance are expensed while betterments that increase capacity, efficiency, or useful life are capitalized.

Depreciation methods

Depreciation allocates depreciable cost (cost − salvage) over the useful life. Illustrative: equipment cost $440,000, salvage $40,000, life 5 years.

  • Straight-line = (cost − salvage) ÷ life = ($440,000 − $40,000) ÷ 5 = $80,000 per year.
  • Double-declining-balance applies twice the straight-line rate (2 ÷ 5 = 40%) to the beginning book value, ignoring salvage until book value nears it: year 1 = 40% × $440,000 = $176,000.
  • Units-of-production allocates by output; sum-of-the-years'-digits is another accelerated method.

Accelerated methods front-load expense (and, in tax, the deduction and its shield), but total depreciation over the life is identical across methods.

Impairment of long-lived assets (ASC 360)

Test a long-lived asset for impairment when indicators exist (declining use, market value drop, adverse changes). The two-step test:

  1. Recoverability: if carrying value exceeds the undiscounted future cash flows, the asset is impaired.
  2. Measurement: impairment loss = carrying value − fair value.

Illustrative: equipment with a carrying value of $300,000 has undiscounted future cash flows of $260,000. Because $300,000 > $260,000, it is impaired. If fair value is $220,000, the impairment loss = $300,000 − $220,000 = $80,000. Note the test uses undiscounted cash flows but the loss is measured to fair value — a classic exam trap. Under US GAAP, impairment losses on assets held for use are not reversed.

Disposals

On disposal, the gain or loss = proceeds − book value (cost − accumulated depreciation). Record depreciation up to the disposal date first. For an asset classified as held for sale, stop depreciating and measure at the lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell.

Capitalized interest, exchanges, and depletion

When an entity constructs an asset for its own use over time, it capitalizes interest on the funds tied up during construction — the avoidable interest, computed on the weighted-average accumulated expenditures, capped at the actual interest incurred for the period. Interest capitalization stops when the asset is substantially complete and ready for use. Nonmonetary exchanges of assets are recorded at fair value (recognizing the full gain or loss) when the exchange has commercial substance — that is, when the future cash flows change as a result; lacking commercial substance, the asset received is recorded at the book value of the asset given up and gains are generally deferred. Natural resources are subject to depletion, typically on a units-of-production basis over the estimated recoverable reserves.

A further obligation, the asset retirement obligation (ARO), arises when law or contract requires the entity to dismantle or restore at the end of an asset's life. The ARO is recognized at the present value of the expected retirement cost, added to the asset's carrying amount, and accreted to its future value over time while the capitalized cost depreciates — a pairing the exam likes to test.

Intangibles, goodwill, and held-for-sale

Intangible assets with finite lives are amortized over their useful lives and tested for impairment like other long-lived assets; those with indefinite lives (and goodwill) are not amortized but are tested for impairment at least annually. Goodwill impairment under current guidance is a one-step test at the reporting-unit level: if the unit's carrying amount exceeds its fair value, the impairment loss equals that excess, limited to the goodwill balance — the older two-step measurement was eliminated. Internally generated goodwill and most internally generated intangibles are not capitalized; research and development is generally expensed as incurred (with specific exceptions for certain software and acquired in-process items).

An asset (or disposal group) is classified as held for sale when management commits to a plan, the asset is available for immediate sale, and the sale is probable within a year. On classification, the entity stops depreciating it and measures it at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell — and, unlike held-for-use impairments, a subsequent recovery in fair value can be recognized up to the previously recognized loss. Together these rules round out the life cycle of long-lived assets from capitalization through use, impairment, and disposal.

Componentization, costs after acquisition, and the IFRS contrast

Two refinements recur. First, costs incurred after acquisition are capitalized only if they extend the asset's useful life, increase its capacity, or improve its efficiency (a betterment); ordinary repairs and maintenance that merely keep the asset operating are expensed. Distinguishing a capital improvement from a repair is a frequent exam judgment with a real cash-and-earnings consequence. Second, under IFRS, significant components of an asset with different useful lives must be depreciated separately (component depreciation) — a roof and the building shell, for instance — whereas US GAAP permits but does not require it.

The IFRS contrast extends to measurement: IFRS allows the revaluation model, carrying PP&E at fair value with increases generally to a revaluation surplus in OCI, and permits reversal of a prior impairment if the asset's value recovers — both prohibited under US GAAP for assets held for use. IFRS also tests impairment in a single step by comparing carrying amount to the higher of fair-value-less-costs-to-sell and value-in-use, using discounted cash flows, where US GAAP's recoverability test uses undiscounted cash flows. Holding these differences straight is the difference between a right and a wrong answer when a question signals which framework applies. In short, US GAAP tests recoverability against undiscounted cash flows and forbids both revaluation and impairment reversal for assets held for use, while IFRS discounts, permits revaluation to a surplus in OCI, and allows reversal — a compact set of contrasts that recurs across the entire FAR blueprint, not only in long-lived assets, and one worth committing to memory as a single block.

CMA bridge

CMA month 11 used straight-line depreciation to compute the tax shield ($80,000 × tax rate); FAR is where the depreciation expense itself, the capitalization rules, and impairment are measured. The numbers tie: the same $80,000 straight-line figure appears in both.

Practice and recap

  1. Capitalize purchase price plus costs to ready the asset; expense repairs, capitalize betterments.
  2. Compute straight-line and double-declining-balance depreciation.
  3. Apply the two-step impairment test: undiscounted cash flows for recoverability, fair value for measurement.
  4. Compute gain/loss on disposal as proceeds minus book value.

Recap: PP&E is recorded at full cost-to-ready, depreciated by a chosen method ($80,000 straight-line or $176,000 first-year double-declining), and written down when carrying value exceeds undiscounted cash flows — with the $80,000 illustrative impairment measured to fair value.

flashcards.back: Purchase price plus all costs to get the asset ready for use (freight, installation, testing, sales tax, capitalized interest).
